items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: Which data structure follows the Last In First Out (LIFO) principle?
items.explanation: A stack removes the most recently added element first — this is the LIFO property.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: In a singly linked list each node contains data and what else?
options: A pointer to the previous node
A pointer to the next node
The total size of the list
items.explanation: Each node in a singly linked list stores data and a reference (pointer) to the next node in the sequence.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: What is the maximum number of children a node can have in a binary tree?
items.explanation: By definition a binary tree node has at most two children: a left child and a right child.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: Which data structure uses First In First Out (FIFO) ordering?
items.explanation: A queue processes elements in the order they were added — the first element enqueued is the first dequeued.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: What does a hash table use to map keys to array indices?
items.explanation: A hash function computes an index from the key so the value can be stored and retrieved in near-constant time.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: Which traversal visits the root node before its subtrees?
items.explanation: Pre-order traversal visits the root first then recursively visits the left subtree followed by the right subtree.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: What is the time complexity of accessing an element by index in an array?
items.explanation: Arrays support constant-time random access because elements are stored in contiguous memory locations.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: What is the worst-case time complexity of inserting into a hash table with chaining?
items.explanation: If all keys hash to the same bucket the chain becomes a linked list of length n so insertion degrades to O(n).

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: Which self-balancing BST guarantees O(log n) height by enforcing a color invariant on every node?
items.explanation: A Red-Black Tree colors every node red or black and enforces rules that keep the longest path at most twice the shortest guaranteeing O(log n) height.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: In a min-heap which element is always at the root?
items.explanation: A min-heap maintains the heap property: every parent is less than or equal to its children so the minimum is always at the root.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: What is the amortized time complexity of appending to a dynamic array that doubles in size when full?
items.explanation: Although individual resizes cost O(n) they happen rarely enough that the amortized cost per append is O(1).

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: Which data structure is best suited for implementing an LRU cache?
items.explanation: An LRU cache needs O(1) lookup (hash map) and O(1) insertion/removal of the least-recently-used item (doubly linked list).

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: What is the space complexity of storing a graph with V vertices and E edges using an adjacency list?
items.explanation: An adjacency list stores a list of neighbors for each vertex using O(V) vertex entries plus O(E) edge entries total.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: After deleting the root of a max-heap how is the heap property restored?
options: Swap root with last element then heapify down
items.explanation: The last element replaces the root then sift-down (heapify) swaps it with its larger child repeatedly until the max-heap property holds.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: A Bloom filter may return false positives but never false negatives. Why is this the case?
options: It uses multiple hash functions mapping to a bit array
It uses a sorted array with binary search
It discards elements after a timeout
items.explanation: A Bloom filter sets bits at multiple hash positions. A lookup checks all positions — an absent element may collide with bits set by other elements (false positive) but a present element always has all its bits set (no false negative).

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: What is the time complexity of building a binary heap from an unsorted array using the bottom-up method?
items.explanation: Bottom-up heap construction calls heapify on each non-leaf node. The total work sums to O(n) because most nodes are near the bottom and require few swaps.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: In a B-tree of minimum degree t what is the maximum number of keys a node can hold?
items.explanation: A B-tree node of minimum degree t can hold at most 2t − 1 keys and 2t children. This keeps the tree balanced and optimizes disk reads.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: Which data structure supports union and find operations in nearly O(1) amortized time using path compression and union by rank?
items.explanation: Union-Find with path compression and union by rank achieves an amortized time complexity of O(α(n)) per operation where α is the inverse Ackermann function — effectively constant.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: What problem does a skip list solve compared to a standard sorted linked list?
items.explanation: A skip list adds multiple levels of forward pointers to a sorted linked list enabling binary-search-like behavior with O(log n) expected time for search insert and delete.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: In a segment tree built over an array of n elements how many nodes does the tree contain in the worst case?
items.explanation: A segment tree is typically allocated as a complete binary tree. For n elements the array representation may need up to 4n nodes to handle non-power-of-two sizes safely.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: What is the key advantage of a Fibonacci heap over a binary heap for Dijkstra's algorithm?
items.explanation: Fibonacci heaps support decrease-key in O(1) amortized time reducing Dijkstra's total complexity to O(V log V + E) compared to O((V+E) log V) with a binary heap.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: What does Big-O notation describe about an algorithm?
options: The exact running time in seconds
An upper bound on growth rate as input size increases
items.explanation: Big-O gives an asymptotic upper bound on how an algorithm's time or space requirements grow relative to input size.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: Which sorting algorithm repeatedly finds the minimum element and places it at the beginning?
items.explanation: Selection sort scans the unsorted portion for the minimum element and swaps it into the next sorted position on each pass.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: What is the time complexity of linear search in the worst case?
items.explanation: Linear search checks each element one by one — in the worst case the target is last or absent requiring n comparisons.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: Binary search requires the input array to be in what state?
items.explanation: Binary search halves the search space at each step which only works correctly when the array is sorted.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: Which algorithm technique solves a problem by breaking it into smaller subproblems solving each recursively and combining results?
items.explanation: Divide and conquer splits the problem into independent subproblems solves them recursively and merges the solutions.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: What is the time complexity of Bubble Sort in the worst case?
items.explanation: Bubble sort makes n passes through the array swapping adjacent elements — nested loops give O(n²) in the worst case.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: Which search algorithm works by checking every element one by one from start to end?
items.explanation: Linear search iterates through the collection sequentially comparing each element with the target.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: What is the average-case time complexity of Quick Sort?
items.explanation: Quick sort's average case partitions the array into roughly equal halves at each level of recursion giving O(n log n) comparisons.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: Which algorithmic paradigm stores solutions to overlapping subproblems to avoid redundant computation?
items.explanation: Dynamic programming identifies overlapping subproblems and stores their results (memoization or tabulation) so each subproblem is solved only once.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: In Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm why must all edge weights be non-negative?
options: The greedy choice assumes shorter partial paths remain shorter
The algorithm only works on trees
items.explanation: Dijkstra greedily finalizes the shortest known distance to a node. A negative edge could later provide a shorter path to an already-finalized node violating this greedy invariant.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: What is the recurrence relation for Merge Sort?
items.explanation: Merge sort splits the array into two halves (2 subproblems of size n/2) and merges them in O(n) time.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: Which graph traversal algorithm uses a queue and visits nodes level by level?
items.explanation: BFS uses a FIFO queue to explore all neighbors at the current depth before moving to the next level.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: A greedy algorithm for the activity selection problem sorts activities by what criterion?
items.explanation: Sorting by finish time and always picking the next compatible activity yields the maximum number of non-overlapping activities — a classic greedy strategy.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: What is the worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort and when does it occur?
options: O(n log n) when the array is sorted
O(n²) when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element
O(n) when all elements are equal
O(n²) when the array is random
items.explanation: If the pivot consistently produces maximally unbalanced partitions (e.g. already sorted array with first-element pivot) recursion depth reaches n and total work becomes O(n²).

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: What is the time complexity of the Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) string matching algorithm?
items.explanation: KMP preprocesses the pattern to build a failure function in O(m) then scans the text in O(n) — total O(n + m) without backtracking on the text.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: Which problem is solved by finding a Hamiltonian cycle of minimum total weight in a complete graph?
items.explanation: The TSP asks for the minimum-cost tour visiting every vertex exactly once and returning to the start — a Hamiltonian cycle of minimum weight.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: What does the Master Theorem directly solve?
options: Recurrences of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)
items.explanation: The Master Theorem applies to divide-and-conquer recurrences where the problem splits into a subproblems each of size n/b with combine cost f(n).

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: In the context of NP-completeness what does a polynomial-time reduction from problem A to problem B prove?
options: B is at least as hard as A
A and B have the same solution
B can be solved in polynomial time
items.explanation: If A ≤ₚ B then any polynomial-time algorithm for B would also solve A — so B is at least as hard as A.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: Which algorithm finds the strongly connected components of a directed graph in O(V + E) time?
items.explanation: Tarjan's SCC algorithm uses a single DFS pass with a stack and low-link values to identify all strongly connected components in linear time.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: What is the time complexity of the Floyd-Warshall all-pairs shortest path algorithm?
items.explanation: Floyd-Warshall uses three nested loops over V vertices to consider every intermediate vertex for every pair giving O(V³).

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: In a maximum-flow network what does the max-flow min-cut theorem state?
options: Maximum flow equals minimum edge weight
Maximum flow equals the capacity of the minimum cut
Maximum flow equals the number of paths
Flow is always equal to demand
items.explanation: The theorem proves that the value of the maximum flow from source to sink equals the total capacity of the edges in the minimum s-t cut.

items.subject: DBMS
items.stem: What does SQL stand for?
items.explanation: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for managing and querying relational databases.

items.subject: DBMS
items.stem: Which SQL keyword is used to retrieve data from a database?
items.explanation: The SELECT statement queries one or more tables and returns the matching rows as a result set.

items.subject: DBMS
items.stem: A primary key in a relational database must be what?
items.explanation: A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table and by definition cannot contain NULL values.

items.subject: DBMS
items.stem: Which type of database relationship links one record in table A to many records in table B?
items.explanation: A one-to-many relationship means a single row in table A can relate to multiple rows in table B — for example one department having many employees.

items.subject: DBMS
items.stem: What does the WHERE clause do in a SQL query?
options: Filters rows based on a condition
items.explanation: The WHERE clause specifies a condition that each row must satisfy to be included in the query results.

items.subject: DBMS
items.stem: Which SQL command is used to add a new row to a table?
items.explanation: INSERT INTO adds a new row of data to an existing table.

items.subject: DBMS
items.stem: What is a foreign key?
options: A column that references the primary key of another table
A unique identifier within the same table
items.explanation: A foreign key creates a link between two tables by referencing the primary key in the parent table enforcing referential integrity.

items.subject: DBMS
items.stem: What is the purpose of database normalization?
options: To reduce data redundancy and improve integrity
items.explanation: Normalization organizes tables to minimize duplicate data and dependency anomalies — each fact is stored in exactly one place.

items.subject: DBMS
items.stem: Which normal form eliminates transitive dependencies?
items.explanation: 3NF requires that every non-key attribute depends only on the primary key — not transitively through another non-key attribute.

items.subject: DBMS
items.stem: What is the ACID property 'Atomicity' in database transactions?
options: All transactions run at the same time
Transactions are isolated from each other
items.explanation: Atomicity guarantees that either all operations in a transaction complete successfully or none of them take effect — partial execution is impossible.

items.subject: DBMS
items.stem: Which type of SQL JOIN returns only the rows with matching values in both tables?
items.explanation: An INNER JOIN returns only those rows where the join condition is satisfied in both tables — unmatched rows are excluded.

items.subject: DBMS
items.stem: What does a database index primarily improve?
items.explanation: An index creates a sorted data structure (like a B-tree) that lets the database locate rows much faster than scanning the entire table.

items.subject: DBMS
items.stem: In a relational database what is a view?
options: A physical copy of a table
A virtual table defined by a stored query
items.explanation: A view is a named SELECT query that behaves like a table but does not store data itself — it dynamically retrieves data when queried.

items.subject: DBMS
items.stem: What is a deadlock in database systems?
options: A query that takes too long
Two transactions waiting for each other's locks indefinitely
items.explanation: A deadlock occurs when transaction A holds lock X and waits for lock Y while transaction B holds Y and waits for X — neither can proceed.

items.subject: DBMS
items.stem: What is the difference between a clustered and a non-clustered index?
options: Clustered indexes are faster; non-clustered are slower
A clustered index determines physical row order; a non-clustered index uses a separate structure pointing to rows
Clustered indexes work on views; non-clustered indexes work on tables
items.explanation: A clustered index sorts and stores table rows by the index key (one per table). A non-clustered index maintains a separate B-tree with pointers back to the data rows.

items.subject: DBMS
items.stem: In the context of ACID what does the Isolation level 'Serializable' guarantee?
options: Transactions execute as if they were run one after another
items.explanation: Serializable is the strictest isolation level — it ensures concurrent transactions produce the same result as some serial execution order preventing all anomalies.

items.subject: DBMS
items.stem: What problem can occur at the 'Read Committed' isolation level but not at 'Repeatable Read'?
items.explanation: At Read Committed a transaction may see different values for the same row if another transaction commits between reads. Repeatable Read prevents this by locking read rows.

items.subject: DBMS
items.stem: What is a write-ahead log (WAL) and why is it important?
options: A log written after transaction commit for auditing
A log written before changes are applied to disk ensuring crash recovery
items.explanation: WAL writes all modifications to a log file before applying them to data pages. After a crash the log can replay committed changes and undo uncommitted ones.

items.subject: DBMS
items.stem: Which concurrency control protocol uses timestamps to order transactions without locks?
items.explanation: The timestamp ordering protocol assigns a unique timestamp to each transaction and ensures read/write operations follow timestamp order — aborting transactions that violate the order.

items.subject: DBMS
items.stem: In query optimization what does a cost-based optimizer use to choose an execution plan?
options: The length of the SQL statement
Statistics about table sizes and index selectivity
The order of columns in the SELECT clause
items.explanation: A cost-based optimizer estimates the I/O and CPU cost of different plans using statistics like row counts histogram distributions and index cardinality to pick the cheapest plan.

items.subject: DBMS
items.stem: What is the CAP theorem in distributed databases?
options: Consistency Availability and Performance can all be achieved
You can guarantee at most two of Consistency Availability and Partition tolerance simultaneously
CAP only applies to NoSQL databases
items.explanation: The CAP theorem states that in the presence of a network partition a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability — it cannot guarantee all three.

items.subject: Operating Systems
items.stem: What is the primary function of an operating system?
options: Manage hardware resources and provide services to applications
items.explanation: An OS acts as an intermediary between applications and hardware — managing CPU memory storage and I/O devices.

items.subject: Operating Systems
items.stem: What is a process in an operating system?
options: A program in execution with its own memory and state
items.explanation: A process is a running instance of a program including its code data stack program counter and allocated resources.

items.subject: Operating Systems
items.stem: Which scheduling algorithm gives each process an equal time slice in round-robin fashion?
items.explanation: Round Robin assigns a fixed time quantum to each process cycling through the ready queue — ensuring fair CPU sharing.

items.subject: Operating Systems
items.stem: What is virtual memory?
options: Memory on an external USB drive
A technique that uses disk space to extend available RAM
items.explanation: Virtual memory maps address spaces to physical RAM and disk so programs can use more memory than physically available. The OS swaps pages between RAM and disk as needed.

items.subject: Operating Systems
items.stem: What is the difference between a thread and a process?
options: A thread is a lightweight unit of execution within a process sharing its memory space
items.explanation: Threads within the same process share code data and resources but each has its own stack and program counter. Processes have separate memory spaces.

items.subject: Operating Systems
items.stem: What does the kernel of an operating system do?
options: Provides the core services including process scheduling and memory management
items.explanation: The kernel is the core component of the OS — it manages CPU scheduling memory allocation device I/O and system calls.

items.subject: Operating Systems
items.stem: What is a system call?
options: A phone call to tech support
An interface for user programs to request services from the OS kernel
items.explanation: System calls provide a controlled gateway for user-space programs to request kernel services like file I/O process creation and memory allocation.

items.subject: Operating Systems
items.stem: What is a race condition?
options: When two programs compete for CPU time
When the outcome depends on the unpredictable order of thread execution
When a process runs too fast
items.explanation: A race condition occurs when multiple threads access shared data concurrently and the result depends on the timing of their execution — leading to unpredictable behavior.

items.subject: Operating Systems
items.stem: What is the purpose of a mutex (mutual exclusion lock)?
options: To ensure only one thread accesses a critical section at a time
items.explanation: A mutex prevents concurrent access to a shared resource — a thread must acquire the lock before entering the critical section and release it when done.

items.subject: Operating Systems
items.stem: Which page replacement algorithm is optimal but impractical to implement?
items.explanation: The optimal algorithm replaces the page that will not be used for the longest time in the future. It requires future knowledge making it impractical but useful as a benchmark.

items.subject: Operating Systems
items.stem: What is thrashing in the context of virtual memory?
options: Excessive page faults causing the system to spend more time swapping than executing
items.explanation: Thrashing occurs when the working set of active pages exceeds available physical memory — the OS constantly swaps pages in and out and useful work drops dramatically.

items.subject: Operating Systems
items.stem: What are the four necessary conditions for a deadlock to occur?
options: Mutual exclusion — hold and wait — no preemption — circular wait
Starvation — livelock — priority inversion — race condition
Mutual exclusion — FIFO — aging — round robin
items.explanation: Coffman's conditions state that deadlock requires all four: mutual exclusion hold-and-wait no preemption and circular wait. Preventing any one condition prevents deadlock.

items.subject: Operating Systems
items.stem: What is the difference between preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling?
options: In preemptive scheduling the OS can forcibly suspend a running process; in non-preemptive it cannot
Preemptive scheduling is only for I/O-bound processes
items.explanation: Preemptive schedulers can interrupt a running process (e.g. when its time quantum expires) while non-preemptive schedulers let each process run until it voluntarily yields or completes.

items.subject: Operating Systems
items.stem: What is the purpose of a Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)?
options: To cache virtual-to-physical address translations for faster memory access
items.explanation: The TLB is a hardware cache that stores recent page table entries. On a TLB hit the CPU skips the page table walk — dramatically speeding up memory access.

items.subject: Operating Systems
items.stem: Explain the Banker's algorithm. What type of deadlock strategy does it implement?
items.explanation: The Banker's algorithm is a deadlock avoidance strategy. Before granting a resource request it checks whether the system would remain in a safe state — if not the request is deferred.

items.subject: Operating Systems
items.stem: What is priority inversion and how does priority inheritance solve it?
options: A high-priority process runs first; inheritance gives it more CPU
A low-priority task holding a lock blocks a high-priority task; priority inheritance temporarily raises the lock holder's priority
Priority is inverted when the scheduler fails; inheritance resets it
It only occurs in real-time systems and has no solution
items.explanation: Priority inversion occurs when a medium-priority task preempts a low-priority one that holds a lock needed by a high-priority task. Priority inheritance boosts the lock holder to prevent this.

items.subject: Operating Systems
items.stem: What is the difference between internal and external fragmentation?
options: Internal wastes space inside allocated blocks; external wastes space between allocated blocks
Internal is on disk; external is in RAM
Internal is caused by paging; external is caused by segmentation only
items.explanation: Internal fragmentation occurs when allocated memory exceeds what the process needs (e.g. fixed-size pages). External fragmentation occurs when free memory is scattered in small non-contiguous chunks.

items.subject: Operating Systems
items.stem: How does Copy-on-Write (COW) optimize the fork() system call?
options: It copies the entire process memory immediately
It shares pages between parent and child and copies only when either writes to a page
It avoids creating a child process
It compresses the memory before copying
items.explanation: COW marks shared pages as read-only after fork(). A write triggers a page fault which copies just that page — avoiding the cost of duplicating the entire address space upfront.

items.subject: Operating Systems
items.stem: What is the difference between a monolithic kernel and a microkernel?
options: A monolithic kernel runs all OS services in kernel space; a microkernel runs minimal services in kernel space and the rest in user space
Microkernels are faster because they have fewer features
items.explanation: Monolithic kernels (e.g. Linux) include drivers file systems and networking in kernel mode. Microkernels (e.g. Minix) keep only IPC scheduling and memory management in the kernel — other services run as user processes.

items.subject: Operating Systems
items.stem: What is Bélády's anomaly in page replacement?
options: Adding more pages always reduces page faults
With FIFO replacement increasing the number of page frames can sometimes increase page faults
It means pages are loaded in the wrong order
items.explanation: Bélády's anomaly is counterintuitive: for FIFO page replacement certain reference strings cause more page faults with more frames. Stack-based algorithms like LRU never exhibit this anomaly.

items.subject: Operating Systems
items.stem: In a real-time operating system what is the difference between hard and soft real-time constraints?
options: Hard real-time requires deadlines to be met absolutely; soft real-time allows occasional deadline misses
Soft real-time is only for multimedia
items.explanation: In hard real-time systems (e.g. aircraft control) missing a deadline is a system failure. Soft real-time (e.g. video streaming) tolerates occasional misses with degraded quality.

items.subject: Computer Networks
items.stem: What does IP stand for in networking?
items.explanation: The Internet Protocol (IP) is responsible for addressing and routing packets across networks to their destination.

items.subject: Computer Networks
items.stem: Which layer of the OSI model is responsible for end-to-end data transfer and error recovery?
items.explanation: The Transport layer (Layer 4) provides reliable end-to-end communication through segmentation flow control and error recovery — e.g. TCP.

items.subject: Computer Networks
items.stem: What is the purpose of DNS in networking?
options: To translate domain names into IP addresses
items.explanation: The Domain Name System maps human-readable domain names (like google.com) to IP addresses so browsers can locate servers.

items.subject: Computer Networks
items.stem: What is the difference between TCP and UDP?
options: TCP provides reliable ordered delivery while UDP is connectionless and faster but unreliable
UDP is used only for email
TCP does not use IP addresses
items.explanation: TCP ensures packets arrive in order with error checking and retransmission. UDP sends packets without guarantees — useful for real-time applications like video calls.

items.subject: Computer Networks
items.stem: What does a router do in a computer network?
options: Forwards data packets between different networks based on IP addresses
items.explanation: A router examines the destination IP of each packet and forwards it toward its destination using routing tables.

items.subject: Computer Networks
items.stem: What is a MAC address?
options: A unique hardware identifier assigned to a network interface card
The same as an IP address
items.explanation: A MAC (Media Access Control) address is a 48-bit hardware address burned into a NIC — used for communication within a local network segment.

items.subject: Computer Networks
items.stem: What is a subnet mask used for?
options: To determine which portion of an IP address identifies the network vs. the host
items.explanation: A subnet mask separates the network prefix from the host portion of an IP address allowing routers to determine if a destination is local or remote.

items.subject: Computer Networks
items.stem: What is the three-way handshake in TCP?
options: The SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK sequence used to establish a TCP connection
A way to terminate a connection
items.explanation: The client sends SYN the server replies with SYN-ACK and the client confirms with ACK. This establishes a reliable connection before data transfer begins.

items.subject: Computer Networks
items.stem: What is the purpose of ARP (Address Resolution Protocol)?
options: To resolve an IP address to a MAC address on a local network
To route packets across the internet
items.explanation: When a host knows the destination IP but needs the MAC address for the local link it broadcasts an ARP request. The target replies with its MAC address.

items.subject: Computer Networks
items.stem: What is NAT (Network Address Translation) used for?
options: To allow multiple devices on a private network to share a single public IP address
items.explanation: NAT translates private IP addresses to a public IP for outgoing traffic and maps responses back — enabling many devices to access the internet through one public address.

items.subject: Computer Networks
items.stem: What is the difference between a hub and a switch?
options: A hub broadcasts to all ports while a switch forwards frames only to the destination port
A switch is wireless and a hub is wired
items.explanation: A hub is a simple repeater that sends incoming frames to every port. A switch learns MAC addresses and forwards frames only to the correct port — reducing collisions.

items.subject: Computer Networks
items.stem: What is CIDR notation and why is it used?
options: A compact representation of IP address ranges (e.g. 192.168.1.0/24) that enables flexible subnetting
items.explanation: CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) replaces the rigid Class A/B/C system allowing networks to be subdivided into subnets of any size by specifying the prefix length.

items.subject: Computer Networks
items.stem: How does DHCP assign IP addresses to devices on a network?
options: By reading the device's MAC address only
items.explanation: A DHCP client broadcasts a Discover message. The server responds with an Offer. The client sends a Request and the server confirms with an Acknowledge — dynamically assigning an IP.

items.subject: Computer Networks
items.stem: What does a firewall do?
options: Monitors and filters incoming and outgoing network traffic based on security rules
items.explanation: A firewall inspects packets against a set of rules and decides whether to allow or block traffic — protecting networks from unauthorized access and attacks.

items.subject: Computer Networks
items.stem: How does TCP handle congestion control?
options: Through algorithms like Slow Start and Congestion Avoidance that dynamically adjust the sending rate
items.explanation: TCP starts with a small congestion window (slow start) doubling it each RTT until loss occurs. Then it switches to congestion avoidance (additive increase) and halves the window on loss (multiplicative decrease).

items.subject: Computer Networks
items.stem: What is the difference between distance-vector and link-state routing protocols?
options: Distance-vector routers share routing tables with neighbors; link-state routers flood topology information to all routers
items.explanation: Distance-vector protocols (e.g. RIP) exchange distance tables with direct neighbors. Link-state protocols (e.g. OSPF) flood link-state advertisements so every router builds a complete topology map and runs Dijkstra.

items.subject: Computer Networks
items.stem: What is BGP and why is it called the 'protocol of the internet'?
options: The Border Gateway Protocol — it manages routing between autonomous systems that make up the internet
items.explanation: BGP is the exterior gateway protocol that enables autonomous systems (ISPs and large networks) to exchange reachability information — forming the global internet routing table.

items.subject: Computer Networks
items.stem: How does TLS (Transport Layer Security) establish a secure connection?
options: Through a handshake that negotiates cipher suites exchanges certificates and derives session keys
By using UDP instead of TCP
items.explanation: The TLS handshake includes: client hello → server hello + certificate → key exchange → session key derivation. This establishes an encrypted channel before application data flows.

items.subject: Computer Networks
items.stem: What is the count-to-infinity problem in distance-vector routing?
options: After a link failure routers slowly increment distance metrics through update loops before converging
items.explanation: When a link fails distance-vector protocols can enter a loop where routers keep incrementing the cost metric — converging very slowly. Solutions include split horizon and poison reverse.

items.subject: Computer Networks
items.stem: What is the purpose of the sliding window protocol in TCP?
options: To allow the sender to transmit multiple segments before requiring an acknowledgment improving throughput
items.explanation: The sliding window allows multiple unacknowledged segments to be in flight. The window size adjusts based on receiver capacity (flow control) and network conditions (congestion control).

items.subject: Computer Networks
items.stem: How does an ARP spoofing attack work and what is its impact?
options: It floods the network with DNS requests
An attacker sends fake ARP replies to associate their MAC with a victim's IP enabling man-in-the-middle attacks
items.explanation: ARP has no authentication. An attacker can send unsolicited ARP replies mapping a legitimate IP to their own MAC — intercepting traffic intended for that IP.

items.subject: OOP
items.stem: What is encapsulation in object-oriented programming?
options: Bundling data and methods that operate on that data into a single unit (class) and restricting direct access
items.explanation: Encapsulation hides internal state behind methods — external code interacts through a public interface without knowing the implementation details.

items.subject: OOP
items.stem: What is inheritance in OOP?
options: A mechanism where a new class derives properties and behavior from an existing class
items.explanation: Inheritance allows a child class to reuse and extend the functionality of a parent class — promoting code reuse and hierarchical design.

items.subject: OOP
items.stem: What is polymorphism?
options: The ability of different classes to be treated through the same interface while behaving differently
items.explanation: Polymorphism lets a method call behave differently depending on the object's actual type — e.g. calling draw() on a Circle vs. a Rectangle produces different results.

items.subject: OOP
items.stem: What is a class in OOP?
options: A blueprint for creating objects that defines attributes and methods
items.explanation: A class defines the structure (attributes) and behavior (methods) that its instances (objects) will have.

items.subject: OOP
items.stem: What is the difference between a class and an object?
options: A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance of that class
items.explanation: A class defines the template. An object is a concrete instance created from that class with its own attribute values stored in memory.

items.subject: OOP
items.stem: What is a constructor?
options: A special method called automatically when an object is created to initialize its state
items.explanation: A constructor initializes the object's attributes when it is instantiated — e.g. __init__ in Python or the class-named method in Java/C++.

items.subject: OOP
items.stem: What does the 'this' (or 'self') keyword refer to in a method?
options: The current instance of the class on which the method is called
items.explanation: 'this' (Java/C++) or 'self' (Python) refers to the specific object invoking the method — allowing access to its own attributes and other methods.

items.subject: OOP
items.stem: What is the difference between method overloading and method overriding?
options: Overloading defines multiple methods with the same name but different parameters in the same class; overriding redefines a parent method in a child class
Overriding requires a new class name
items.explanation: Overloading is compile-time polymorphism (same method name different signatures). Overriding is runtime polymorphism (child replaces parent's method with its own implementation).

items.subject: OOP
items.stem: What is an abstract class?
options: A class that cannot be instantiated and may contain abstract methods that subclasses must implement
A class that is automatically deleted
items.explanation: Abstract classes define a contract — they can have both implemented and abstract (unimplemented) methods. Subclasses must provide implementations for the abstract methods.

items.subject: OOP
items.stem: What is the difference between an interface and an abstract class?
options: An interface declares method signatures without implementation (prior to Java 8); an abstract class can include both implemented and abstract methods
items.explanation: Interfaces define a pure contract. Abstract classes can share common code. A class can implement multiple interfaces but typically extends only one abstract class.

items.subject: OOP
items.stem: What is the SOLID principle 'Single Responsibility'?
options: A class should have only one method
A class should have only one reason to change
A variable should hold only one value
A function should have only one parameter
items.explanation: The Single Responsibility Principle states each class should be responsible for one aspect of functionality — reducing coupling and making changes localized.

items.subject: OOP
items.stem: What is composition in OOP and how does it differ from inheritance?
options: Composition is the same as inheritance
Composition builds complex objects by containing instances of other classes rather than inheriting from them
items.explanation: Composition uses a 'has-a' relationship (a Car has an Engine) while inheritance uses an 'is-a' relationship (a Dog is an Animal). Composition is generally more flexible.

items.subject: OOP
items.stem: What is the purpose of access modifiers like public private and protected?
options: To control the visibility and accessibility of class members
items.explanation: Access modifiers enforce encapsulation: private restricts access to the class itself protected adds access for subclasses and public allows access from anywhere.

items.subject: OOP
items.stem: What is a design pattern in OOP?
options: A reusable solution template for a commonly occurring software design problem
items.explanation: Design patterns (like Singleton Factory Observer) provide proven approaches to recurring design challenges — they are not code but templates for how to structure solutions.

items.subject: OOP
items.stem: What is the Liskov Substitution Principle and why does violating it cause bugs?
options: Subclasses should always override all parent methods
Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of a subclass without altering program correctness
It requires all classes to be abstract
items.explanation: LSP means subclasses must honor the contract of their parent. Violating it (e.g. a Square subclass of Rectangle that breaks setWidth/setHeight expectations) causes subtle bugs when code uses the parent type.

items.subject: OOP
items.stem: What problem does the Dependency Inversion Principle solve?
options: High-level modules depending on low-level implementation details making the system rigid
items.explanation: DIP states that high-level modules should depend on abstractions not concretions. This allows swapping implementations (e.g. switching databases) without modifying business logic.

items.subject: OOP
items.stem: How does the Observer pattern work and when should it be used?
options: Subjects maintain a list of observers and notify them of state changes — useful for event-driven architectures
items.explanation: The Observer pattern decouples event producers from consumers. When the subject's state changes all registered observers are automatically notified — used in GUIs event systems and reactive programming.

items.subject: OOP
items.stem: What is the diamond problem in multiple inheritance and how do languages solve it?
options: Ambiguity when a class inherits from two classes that share a common ancestor — solved by virtual inheritance or interfaces
items.explanation: If class D inherits from B and C which both inherit from A then D has two copies of A's members. C++ uses virtual inheritance; Java/C# avoid the problem by allowing only single class inheritance with multiple interfaces.

items.subject: OOP
items.stem: What is the difference between shallow copy and deep copy of an object?
options: A shallow copy duplicates the object but shares references to nested objects; a deep copy recursively duplicates all nested objects
items.explanation: With a shallow copy modifying a nested object in the copy also affects the original. Deep copy creates fully independent copies at all levels — important for mutable nested structures.

items.subject: OOP
items.stem: How does the Strategy pattern differ from the Template Method pattern?
options: Strategy uses composition to swap entire algorithms at runtime; Template Method uses inheritance to let subclasses override specific steps
items.explanation: Strategy encapsulates algorithms as interchangeable objects (composition). Template Method defines a skeleton algorithm in a base class with hook methods that subclasses override (inheritance).

items.subject: OOP
items.stem: What is type erasure in Java generics and what are its implications?
options: Generics are erased at compile time
Generic type information is removed at runtime by the compiler — preventing runtime type checks on generic parameters
Generics are always preserved at runtime
Type erasure only affects primitive types
items.explanation: Java compiles generics by replacing type parameters with their bounds (usually Object) and inserting casts. This means you cannot do instanceof on generic types or create generic arrays at runtime.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: What is the maximum number of children any node can have in a binary tree?
items.explanation: By definition, a binary tree is a hierarchical data structure in which each node has at most two children, referred to as the left child and the right child.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: What is a node called if it has no child nodes?
items.explanation: Nodes at the bottom of the tree structure that do not have any children are called leaf nodes or external nodes.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: Which traversal visits nodes in the order: Left Subtree, Right Subtree, Root?
items.explanation: Post-order traversal recursively visits the left subtree, then the right subtree, and finally processes the root node.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: In a standard Binary Search Tree (BST) containing unique values, the left child of a node must have a value that is:
options: Greater than the parent node's value
Less than the parent node's value
Equal to the parent node's value
items.explanation: The fundamental property of a BST is that for any given node, all elements in its left subtree are smaller than the node, and all elements in its right subtree are larger.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: Which binary tree traversal of a Binary Search Tree (BST) produces the keys in sorted ascending order?
items.explanation: An in-order traversal (Left, Root, Right) of a Binary Search Tree visits values in non-decreasing order because of the underlying BST properties.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: What is the maximum number of nodes at level L of a binary tree, assuming the root is at level 0?
items.explanation: At each successive level of a binary tree, the capacity of nodes doubles. Level 0 has 1 (2^0) node, Level 1 has 2 (2^1) nodes, Level 2 has 4 (2^2) nodes, resulting in 2^L nodes at level L.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: A binary tree in which every node other than the leaves has exactly two children is known as a:
items.explanation: A Full Binary Tree (sometimes called a strict binary tree) is a tree structure where every node has either 0 or 2 children.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: What is the depth of the root node in a standard binary tree representation?
options: It depends on the total height
items.explanation: The depth of a node is the number of edges from the node to the tree's root node. Since the root node is its own ancestor, the edge count is 0.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: Which data structure is most appropriate to perform a Level-Order (Breadth-First) traversal of a binary tree?
items.explanation: Level-order traversal visits nodes level by level from left to right. A Queue (FIFO) is used to track visited nodes and process their children in correct sequential order.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: What is a binary tree called where every level, except possibly the last, is completely filled, and all nodes in the last level are as far left as possible?
items.explanation: A complete binary tree has all levels completely filled except potentially the last level, which must be filled from left to right without any gaps.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: If a binary tree has N nodes, how many null (empty) pointers does it contain?
items.explanation: A binary tree with N nodes has 2N total child pointers. Since N-1 nodes have incoming parent pointers (all except the root), the number of empty/null pointers is 2N - (N - 1) = N + 1.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: What is the height of a perfect binary tree containing 15 nodes? (Assume the height of a single-node tree is 0)
items.explanation: A perfect binary tree with height h contains 2^(h+1) - 1 nodes. For 15 nodes: 2^(h+1) - 1 = 15 => 2^(h+1) = 16 => h+1 = 4 => h = 3.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: You are given the pre-order traversal sequence [A, B, D, E, C, F] and the in-order traversal sequence [D, B, E, A, F, C] of a binary tree. What is its post-order traversal?
items.explanation: The root is A (from pre-order). In-order shows left subtree elements [D, B, E] and right subtree elements [F, C]. Reconstructing the left tree gives B as root, D as left, E as right. Reconstructing the right tree gives C as root, F as left. The post-order sequence is Left-Right-Root: [D, E, B, F, C, A].

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: Which of the following operations cannot be performed in O(log N) worst-case time on a self-balancing binary search tree (like an AVL tree) containing N nodes?
options: Finding the successor of a node
items.explanation: Sorting all elements requires visiting all N nodes, which takes O(N) time. Searching, inserting, and finding a successor in a self-balancing BST all operate within O(log N) height limits.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: In a standard binary search tree (BST), what is the worst-case time complexity of searching for an element if the tree is unbalanced?
items.explanation: In an unbalanced BST, the tree can degenerate into a linear sequence (skewed tree). Searching in a skewed tree of N elements requires checking every node, yielding O(N) worst-case time complexity.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: If you insert the keys [10, 20, 30, 40, 50] in that exact order into an initially empty, unbalanced BST, what structure is formed?
items.explanation: Each subsequent key is strictly larger than all preceding keys. Therefore, each new node will be inserted as the right child of the previously inserted node, forming a linear rightward-slanted line.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: To find the Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) of two nodes, p and q, in a Binary Search Tree (BST) containing unique elements, which heuristic property can you exploit?
options: The LCA is the node whose value lies strictly between the values of p and q (inclusive)
The LCA is always the root node
The LCA is the node with the highest numerical height value
The LCA is the leaf node closest to both p and q
items.explanation: In a BST, if you traverse from the root, the first node you encounter whose value splits the path (i.e., its value is between p and q inclusive) is their Lowest Common Ancestor.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: What is the maximum number of leaf nodes in a binary tree of height h? (Assume height of a single-node tree is 0)
items.explanation: The maximum number of leaves is achieved when the tree is a perfect binary tree. At height h, the bottommost level (level h) contains exactly 2^h nodes, all of which are leaves.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: What defines a threaded binary tree?
options: A tree where each node has a pointer to its parent node
A tree where null pointers are replaced with pointers to their in-order predecessor or successor
A tree optimized for execution on multi-threaded computer systems
A tree where nodes are structurally laid out in contiguous array memory blocks
items.explanation: A threaded binary tree replaces standard empty child pointers (nulls) with 'threads' linking directly to the in-order predecessor or successor to facilitate traversal without stack/recursion overhead.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: Which single traversal sequence is sufficient on its own to completely reconstruct a unique binary tree, provided we serialize null child nodes?
items.explanation: Standard pre-order (or post-order/level-order) traversals require an accompanying in-order traversal to reconstruct a unique tree. However, if null child markers are preserved, pre-order alone contains sufficient structural depth information.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: How many structurally unique Binary Search Trees (BSTs) can be formed containing exactly n distinct keys?
items.explanation: The number of structurally unique BSTs with n distinct keys is calculated by the Catalan Number sequence, given by the formula C_n = (1 / (n + 1)) * (2n Choose n).

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: When implementing an iterative post-order traversal of a binary tree using a single stack, which of the following actions is necessary to determine if we should process a parent node?
options: Track the last visited node to check if we just returned from its right subtree
Check if the stack depth is currently odd or even
Verify that both child pointers of the top stack node are null
Convert the tree nodes into a queue sequence first
items.explanation: In post-order traversal, the root is visited after both subtrees. Using one stack, you can only pop and process the root when returning from its right child (or if the right child is null/empty). Tracking the 'last visited' node validates this state.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: In a strict (full) binary tree where every node has either 0 or 2 children, if there are L leaf nodes, how many internal nodes (I) does the tree have?
items.explanation: In any full binary tree, the relationship between the number of leaves (L) and the number of internal nodes (I) is strictly L = I + 1. Rearranging this yields I = L - 1.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: What is the optimal time complexity of finding the diameter of an arbitrary binary tree?
items.explanation: The naive recursive approach calculates height at each step, taking O(N^2). However, an optimized bottom-up approach calculates height and diameter simultaneously in a single post-order pass, reducing the complexity to O(N).

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: To perform an in-place conversion of a binary tree to a sorted doubly linked list (matching in-order sequence), recursive functions typically keep track of which references?
options: The depth level of the recursion to offset pointer arrays
The head and tail pointers of the previously converted sublists
Parent pointers and subtree sibling nodes
The overall median value of the original tree
items.explanation: To perform an in-place conversion, you recursively convert the left and right subtrees and then link the root with the tail of the left list and the head of the right list. Hence, maintaining head and tail references is necessary.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: In an AVL tree, after inserting a node, you detect an unbalanced node with a balance factor of -2 (right-heavy). Its right child has a balance factor of +1 (left-heavy). Which rotation sequence is required?
items.explanation: When the parent node is right-heavy (-2) and its child is left-heavy (+1), this represents a Right-Left (RL) mismatch. A right rotation is performed on the child node first, followed by a left rotation on the unbalanced parent node.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: When finding the maximum path sum in a binary tree (where the path can start and end at any node), what is the correct formula to update the global maximum tracker 'global_max' at a node 'u' with computed maximum downward path branches 'left_down' and 'right_down'?
options: global_max = max(global_max, u.val + max(0, left_down) + max(0, right_down))
items.explanation: The maximum path containing node 'u' as its highest node joins 'u' with any non-negative contribution from its left and right downward paths. Thus, we check u.val + max(0, left_down) + max(0, right_down) against the global tracker.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: What is the worst-case space complexity of a recursive Depth-First Search (DFS) traversal of an arbitrary binary tree with N nodes?
items.explanation: In a completely skewed tree, the call stack grows proportional to the height of the tree. Since the height in the worst-case scenario can equal N (when the tree is basically a single branch), the space complexity is O(N).

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: If you want to serialize a binary tree into a string using Level-Order (BFS) traversal, how must you handle missing children to ensure lossless deserialization?
options: You can skip storing null indicators if you write values to a binary file
You must store placeholder null markers for empty child branches of visited nodes
Omit null pointers and rely on sorting keys upon loading
BFS cannot support lossless serialization because it lacks parent indicators
items.explanation: Without maintaining null placeholder symbols (e.g., '#') for missing child links during level-order queue processing, it is impossible to reconstruct the correct parent-child topology during reconstruction.

items.subject: Data Structures
items.stem: To find the in-order successor of a node x in a binary search tree where each node possesses a parent pointer, if x has no right child, how do you locate the successor?
options: The successor is the left child of x's parent node
The successor is the deepest leftmost leaf node in the left subtree of x
The successor is the lowest ancestor of x whose left child is also an ancestor of x
The successor does not exist because there is no right child
items.explanation: Without a right child, the in-order successor must be an ancestor. We traverse upward via parent pointers; the first node we reach from its left child is the in-order successor.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: What is the primary role of the base case in a recursive function?
options: To call the function with a modified argument
To terminate the recursion and prevent infinite loops
To allocate dynamic memory on the heap
To increase the execution speed of the program
items.explanation: The base case is a critical boundary condition that stops the recursion from proceeding indefinitely, avoiding call stack overflow.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: Which error occurs when a recursive function fails to reach its base case, leading to unlimited calls?
items.explanation: Each recursive call consumes frame space on the call stack. Without a terminating base case, memory limit is exceeded, triggering a StackOverflowError.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: Which internal data structure is utilized by the runtime environment to track active recursive subroutine calls?
items.explanation: The call stack manages active subroutines, pushing stack frames containing local variables and return addresses for each recursive execution.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: A standard recursive function must contain which two key components?
options: A loop and a break statement
A base case and a recursive case
A pointer and an allocation step
A try block and a catch block
items.explanation: Every proper recursive algorithm requires at least one base case to stop execution, and a recursive step to progress toward the base case.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: What is direct recursion?
options: A function calling another function which then calls the original
A loop converting itself into a stack frame
A recursive function optimized to run in O(1) space
items.explanation: Direct recursion occurs when a function explicitly contains a call to itself within its own body.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: If a countdown function countdown(n) prints n and then calls countdown(n-1) when n > 0, what will countdown(3) print if the print statement runs before the recursive call?
items.explanation: Since the print statement runs before the recursive step, the numbers are printed in descending order: 3, then 2, then 1, stopping when n becomes 0.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: What is the return value of a recursive factorial function fact(n) for fact(3) if fact(n) = n * fact(n-1) with base case fact(0) = 1?
items.explanation: fact(3) evaluates as 3 * fact(2) = 3 * 2 * fact(1) = 3 * 2 * 1 * fact(0) = 3 * 2 * 1 * 1 = 6.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: What happens if a recursive function does not make progress toward its base case on each step?
options: It causes an infinite loop / stack overflow
It automatically switches to an iterative equivalent
items.explanation: Without progression toward the base case, the termination criteria are never met, resulting in endless recursion and stack depletion.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: In recursive terminology, what is the 'recursive step'?
options: The statement that handles the simplest input directly
The line of code that frees call stack frames
The part of the function where the problem is reduced to a smaller subproblem
The compilation step that optimizes recursive loops
items.explanation: The recursive step decomposes the primary problem into a smaller, solvable instance of the same problem.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: What is the worst-case space complexity of a linear recursive algorithm processing N elements with a call stack depth of N (assuming no tail-call optimization)?
items.explanation: Each frame on the call stack takes up constant O(1) space. For N active recursive calls, the space complexity scales linearly to O(N).

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: What is the time complexity of the standard recursive Fibonacci algorithm defined by F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2) without optimization?
items.explanation: The recursion tree for naive Fibonacci branches into two subproblems at each step, yielding an exponential growth rate of roughly O(1.618^N), which is bounded by O(2^N).

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: Which property must a recursive call possess to be classified as 'tail recursive'?
options: It must be the first line of the function
The recursive call must be the final operation evaluated, with no pending work
It must occur inside a loop body
It must return a static variable
items.explanation: Tail recursion requires that the result of the recursive call is directly returned without any further operations (like addition or multiplication) pending.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem:
Consider the following Python function:

```python
def rev(s):
    if len(s) <= 1:
        return s
    return rev(s[1:]) + s[0]
```
What does rev('algo') return?
items.explanation: This algorithm recursively processes the slice s[1:] and appends the first character s[0] at the end, successfully reversing the input string to 'ogla'.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem:
For the Euclidean recursive GCD algorithm:
gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) with base case b == 0 returning a.
How many recursive calls (excluding the initial call) are made to compute gcd(24, 9)?
items.explanation: Initial call: gcd(24, 9). Call 1: gcd(9, 6). Call 2: gcd(6, 3). Call 3: gcd(3, 0) which hits base case. There are 3 recursive calls.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: Which recurrence relation describes the worst-case time complexity of a recursive Binary Search on a sorted array of size N?
items.explanation: Binary search divides the search space in half at each step (T(N/2)) and performs constant-time comparisons (O(1)) at the middle element.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.explanation: foo(3) prints 3, calls foo(2). foo(2) prints 2, calls foo(1). foo(1) prints 1, calls foo(0) (returns). After return, unwinding executes the remaining print statements: 1, then 2, then 3.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem:
How many total calls to fib (including the initial call) are made when calculating the 4th Fibonacci number using: 
fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) with base cases fib(1) = 1 and fib(0) = 0?
items.explanation: Tree of calls: fib(4) -> [fib(3), fib(2)]. fib(3) -> [fib(2), fib(1)]. fib(2) -> [fib(1), fib(0)]. The second fib(2) from fib(4) -> [fib(1), fib(0)]. Total calls: fib(4)[1] + fib(3)[1] + fib(2)[2] + fib(1)[3] + fib(0)[2] = 9.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: What optimization technique stores the results of expensive recursive function calls to avoid redundant computations on identical inputs?
items.explanation: Memoization caches the output of function calls relative to their parameter states, enabling top-down recursive solutions to achieve optimal lookup times (often O(1)) on repeating subproblems.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: Given pow(x, y) = x * pow(x, y-1) with base case pow(x, 0) = 1, what is the runtime of evaluating pow(2, N) linearly, and how can it be optimized recursively to logarithmic time?
options: Linear O(N); optimize using pow(x, y/2) * pow(x, y/2) dividing powers.
Linear O(N^2); optimize using binary division trees.
Linear O(N); optimize using Memoized sliding windows.
Linear O(log N); optimize using tail-call mapping.
items.explanation: Evaluating linearly takes O(N) depth. It can be optimized to O(log N) using divide-and-conquer exponentiation: x^y = (x^(y/2))^2 for even y.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: When recursively computing the height of a binary tree, what is the correct formulation of the recursive case?
items.explanation: The height of a node is 1 (for the current level node) plus the maximum of the heights of its left and right subtrees.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: For the Tower of Hanoi puzzle with N disks, what is the minimum number of moves required, and what is the recurrence relation governing this problem?
options: N^2 moves, governed by T(N) = T(N-1) + N
items.explanation: To move N disks, you must recursively move N-1 disks to an auxiliary peg (T(N-1)), move the largest disk (1 step), and move the N-1 disks to the destination peg (T(N-1)). This yields T(N) = 2T(N-1) + 1, which solves to 2^N - 1.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: In the context of compilation and runtime systems, how does Tail Call Optimization (TCO) prevent Stack Overflow errors during deeply nested tail recursion?
options: It allocates the activation record dynamically on the heap rather than the call stack.
It compiles recursive calls into iterative loops by reusing the current activation record frame.
It forks separate threads to handle each cascading recursive frame concurrently.
It uses an automatic pruning garbage collector to discard previous parent frames.
items.explanation: TCO avoids creating new stack frames for tail-recursive calls by overwriting the current frame with the parameters of the child call, running in O(1) stack space.

items.subject: Algorithms
Algorithms
items.stem: What is mutual (indirect) recursion, and which of the following code blocks demonstrates it?
options: A function calling itself inside a loop
Two or more functions calling each other in a circular chain
A recursive function that utilizes a helper method within its base case
A function calling its own duplicate helper with different parameters
items.explanation: Mutual recursion is a form of recursion where two or more functions are defined in terms of each other (e.g., function A calls B, and B calls A).

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: When analyzing the memory usage of Quick Sort in the worst-case scenario where the chosen pivot is always the smallest or largest element, what is the maximum call stack space complexity?
items.explanation: In the worst case, the partitioning yields subproblems of size 0 and N-1. The recursion depth goes up to N, consuming O(N) space on the call stack.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: The McCarthy 91 function is defined as: M(n) = n - 10 if n > 100, and M(M(n + 11)) if n <= 100. What is the value of M(95)?
items.explanation: For all inputs n <= 100, the McCarthy 91 function returns 91. Tracking M(95) -> M(M(106)) -> M(96) -> M(M(107)) -> M(97)... eventually resolves to 91.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: In a backtracking algorithm to find all permutations of a unique list of size N, what is the upper-bound execution time complexity and total leaf nodes in the recursion tree?
items.explanation: Generating all permutations of size N requires making decisions that scale factorially. There are exactly N! unique permutations, leading to N! leaf nodes in the search tree.

items.stem: What is the worst-case space complexity of a Depth-First Search (DFS) algorithm implemented recursively on a graph with V vertices and E edges?
items.explanation: The recursion stack depth is bounded by the maximum path length from the source. In the worst case (a linear path visiting all vertices), the stack will hold up to V frames, resulting in O(V) space complexity.

items.subject: Algorithms
items.stem: Which of the following describes a nested recursion?
options: A function containing multiple recursive calls in sequence
A recursive function that calls another function inside its base case
A recursive function where a recursive call is passed as an argument to another recursive call
A recursive function containing an iterative loop within its body
items.explanation: Nested recursion occurs when a parameter to a recursive call is itself a recursive call (e.g., f(f(n-1))), as seen in the Ackermann and McCarthy 91 functions.
